introduction: This guide presents ordinary differential equations (ODEs) in a step-by-step format. Each topic is broken down into connected steps that build on the source material, helping you follow the reasoning and methods for solving first-order and second-order ODEs.

sections.title: Study Guide Overview and Learning Objectives
paragraphs: This is a 7-page mathematics study guide with 8 worked examples covering ordinary differential equations (ODEs). The guide is designed to help you understand what an ordinary differential equation is, identify order and degree and distinguish linear from nonlinear equations, solve basic first-order ODEs using separation of variables and integrating factors, recognize and solve simple second-order linear homogeneous equations, and interpret initial conditions and apply them to obtain particular solutions.

sections.title: Introduction to ODEs: Definitions and Classification
paragraphs: An ordinary differential equation is an equation involving an unknown function of one independent variable and one or more of its derivatives. ODEs are used to describe quantities that change with respect to another variable, such as time, distance or position.

evidence.quote:
Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs) • Page 2

1. Introduction to ODEs

An ordinary differential equation is an equation involving an unknown function of one independent variable and one or more of its derivatives. ODEs are used to describe quantities that change with respect to another variable, such as time, distance or position.

Basic terminology

• The order of an ODE is the highest derivative appearing in the equation.

• The degree is the power of the highest-order derivative after the equation has been made polynomial in its

derivatives.

• An ODE is linear if the dependent variable and its derivatives occur only to the first power and are not

multiplied together.

• A solution is a function that satisfies the differential equation on an appropriate interval.

Example 1 — Identify order and degree

• Consider: y''' + 4y'' - y' + 7y = 0.

• The highest derivative is y''', so the order is 3. The highest derivative occurs to the first power, so the

degree is 1.

Example 2 — Classify an ODE

• Consider: y' + 3y = x².

• This is a first-order linear ODE because y and y' occur only to the first power and are not multiplied

together.

steps: Identify the highest derivative appearing in the equation; this determines the order of the ODE.
Find the power of the highest-order derivative after the equation has been made polynomial in its derivatives; this is the degree.
Check if the dependent variable and its derivatives occur only to the first power and are not multiplied together; if so, the ODE is linear.
Verify that a proposed solution is a function that satisfies the differential equation on an appropriate interval.
For Example 1, the highest derivative is y''', so the order is 3, and the highest derivative occurs to the first power, so the degree is 1.
For Example 2, y' + 3y = x² is a first-order linear ODE because y and y' occur only to the first power and are not multiplied together.

sections.title: First-Order ODEs: Separation of Variables
paragraphs: A separable differential equation can be rearranged so that all terms involving the dependent variable are on one side and all terms involving the independent variable are on the other. The general pattern is: if dy/dx = f(x)g(y), rearrange to dy/g(y) = f(x) dx, then integrate both sides.

evidence.quote:
Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs) • Page 3

2. First-Order ODEs: Separation of Variables

A separable differential equation can be rearranged so that all terms involving the dependent variable are on one side and all terms involving the independent variable are on the other.

General pattern

• If dy/dx = f(x)g(y), rearrange to dy/g(y) = f(x) dx, then integrate both sides.

Example 3 — Separable equation

• Solve dy/dx = 3x²y.

• Separate: dy/y = 3x² dx.

• Integrate: ln|y| = x³ + C.

• Therefore: y = Ce^(x³).

Example 4 — Separable equation with an initial condition

• Solve dy/dx = 2xy, given y(0) = 5.

• Separate: dy/y = 2x dx.

• Integrate: ln|y| = x² + C, so y = Ce^(x²).

• Using y(0)=5 gives C=5.

• Therefore: y = 5e^(x²).

steps: Recognize that the equation has the form dy/dx = f(x)g(y), where the right side is a product of a function of x and a function of y.
Rearrange the equation to separate variables: dy/g(y) = f(x) dx.
Integrate both sides of the separated equation.
Solve for y to obtain the general solution.
If an initial condition is given, substitute the initial values to determine the arbitrary constant C.
Write the particular solution using the determined constant.

sections.title: First-Order Linear ODEs: Integrating Factor Method
paragraphs: A first-order linear ODE can be written in the standard form dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x). It is commonly solved using an integrating factor. The integrating factor is μ(x) = e^(∫P(x)dx). Multiplying the equation by μ converts the left-hand side into the derivative of μy.

evidence.quote:
Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs) • Page 4

3. First-Order Linear ODEs

A first-order linear ODE can be written in the standard form dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x). It is commonly solved using an integrating factor.

Integrating factor

• The integrating factor is μ(x) = e^(∫P(x)dx). Multiplying the equation by μ converts the left-hand side into the

derivative of μy.

Example 5 — Integrating factor method

• Solve dy/dx + 2y = 4.

• Here P(x)=2, so μ=e^(∫2dx)=e^(2x).

• Multiply through: e^(2x)y' + 2e^(2x)y = 4e^(2x).

• Thus d/dx(e^(2x)y)=4e^(2x).

• Integrating gives e^(2x)y=2e^(2x)+C.

• Therefore: y=2+Ce^(-2x).

steps: Write the equation in standard form dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x) and identify P(x).
Compute the integrating factor μ(x) = e^(∫P(x)dx).
Multiply the entire equation by the integrating factor μ(x).
Recognize that the left-hand side becomes d/dx(μy).
Integrate both sides to find μy.
Solve for y to obtain the general solution.

sections.title: Applications and Initial-Value Problems
paragraphs: An initial-value problem gives a differential equation together with a condition such as y(xₙ)=yₙ. The condition determines the arbitrary constant in the general solution. An ODE may describe a rate of change. For example, if y represents the amount of a quantity at time t, then dy/dt represents its instantaneous rate of change. An initial condition specifies the starting state.

evidence.quote:
Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs) • Page 5

4. Applications and Initial-Value Problems

An initial-value problem gives a differential equation together with a condition such as y(xn)=yn. The condition determines the arbitrary constant in the general solution.

Example 6 — Initial-value problem

• Solve y' = 6x - 4, given y(1)=3.

• Integrate: y = 3x² - 4x + C.

• Apply y(1)=3: 3 - 4 + C = 3, so C=4.

• Therefore: y = 3x² - 4x + 4.

Common interpretation

• An ODE may describe a rate of change. For example, if y represents the amount of a quantity at time t,

then dy/dt represents its instantaneous rate of change. An initial condition specifies the starting state.

steps: Solve the differential equation to find the general solution containing an arbitrary constant C.
Apply the initial condition by substituting the given values into the general solution.
Solve for the constant C.
Write the particular solution using the determined constant.

sections.title: Second-Order Linear ODEs: Characteristic Equation
paragraphs: A common second-order linear homogeneous ODE has the form ay'' + by' + cy = 0, where a, b and c are constants. We use the characteristic equation to determine the form of the solution. Assume y=e^(rx). Substitution gives the characteristic equation ar²+br+c=0.

evidence.quote:
Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs) • Page 6

5. Second-Order Linear ODEs

A common second-order linear homogeneous ODE has the form ay'' + by' + cy = 0, where a, b and c are constants. We use the characteristic equation to determine the form of the solution.

Characteristic equation

• Assume y=e^(rx). Substitution gives the characteristic equation ar²+br+c=0.

• If the roots are distinct real numbers rn and rn, then y=Cne^(rnx)+Cne^(rnx).

• If there is a repeated root r, then y=(Cn+Cnx)e^(rx).

Example 7 — Distinct roots

• Solve y'' - 5y' + 6y = 0.

• Characteristic equation: r² - 5r + 6 = 0.

• Factor: (r-2)(r-3)=0, giving r=2 and r=3.

• Therefore: y=Cne^(2x)+Cne^(3x).

steps: Write the ODE in the form ay'' + by' + cy = 0 and identify the constants a, b, and c.
Assume a solution of the form y=e^(rx) and substitute into the ODE.
Obtain the characteristic equation ar²+br+c=0.
Solve the characteristic equation for the roots r.
If the roots are distinct real numbers r₁ and r₂, write the general solution as y=C₁e^(r₁x)+C₂e^(r₂x).
If there is a repeated root r, write the general solution as y=(C₁+C₂x)e^(rx).

sections.title: Repeated Roots, Summary and Practice
paragraphs: Repeated roots require a second independent solution containing x. This is one of the important cases in second-order linear ODEs. The guide concludes with a quick revision checklist and key formulas for separable equations, linear first-order equations, and second-order constant coefficient equations.

evidence.quote:
Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs) • Page 7

6. Repeated Roots, Summary and Practice

Repeated roots require a second independent solution containing x. This is one of the important cases in second-order linear ODEs.

Example 8 — Repeated root

• Solve y'' - 4y' + 4y = 0.

• Characteristic equation: r² - 4r + 4 = 0 = (r-2)².

• The repeated root is r=2.

• Therefore: y=(Cn+Cnx)e^(2x).

Quick revision checklist

• Can you identify the order and degree of an ODE?

• Can you recognize a separable equation?

• Can you find an integrating factor for a first-order linear equation?

• Can you apply an initial condition to find an arbitrary constant?

• Can you form and solve a characteristic equation for a second-order homogeneous ODE?

Key formulas

• Separable: dy/g(y) = f(x)dx.

• Linear first order: y' + P(x)y = Q(x), with μ=e^(∫P(x)dx).

• Second-order constant coefficients: ar²+br+c=0.

• Distinct roots: y=Cne^(rnx)+Cne^(rnx).

• Repeated root: y=(Cn+Cnx)e^(rx).

steps: For a repeated root r, recognize that the general solution must include a second independent solution containing x.
Write the solution as y=(C₁+C₂x)e^(rx).
Review the checklist: Can you identify order and degree, recognize separable equations, find integrating factors, apply initial conditions, and solve characteristic equations?
Remember the key formulas: dy/g(y) = f(x)dx for separable equations; y' + P(x)y = Q(x) with μ=e^(∫P(x)dx) for linear first order; ar²+br+c=0 for second-order constant coefficients.
For distinct roots, use y=C₁e^(r₁x)+C₂e^(r₂x); for repeated roots, use y=(C₁+C₂x)e^(rx).
